2027-04-24.verse: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.
theo: Few saints are loved across so many Churches and nations as St George. In the Syriac tradition he is Mar Geevarghese Sahada, George the Martyr; Sahada means witness, the one who bears testimony with his blood. Kerala is full of his churches and his name: in Christian families of every tradition, boys are called Geevarghese, Varghese, Varkey and George, and great pilgrim churches such as Aruvithura and Edathua draw crowds who come to him with their fears and their vows. What do we know of him? The early Church honoured his tomb at Lydda, the town in Palestine where Peter once healed Aeneas, and pilgrims were visiting it by the sixth century. The tradition remembers him as a soldier in the Roman army who refused to deny Christ in the great persecution under the emperor Diocletian, at the beginning of the fourth century, and who was tortured and beheaded. An ancient list of writings, attributed to Pope Gelasius at the end of the fifth century but probably compiled somewhat later, named him among those saints whose names are rightly honoured but whose deeds are known only to God. The famous story of the dragon came much later, in the Middle Ages, and is a legend, not history; the Church reads it as a picture of the truth, that the martyr's faith overcomes the ancient serpent. The history is short, but it is enough: a man under orders, with everything to lose, who chose Christ above his career and his life.

The readings chosen for the feast gather around that choice. Daniel, a Jewish exile serving the king of the Medes and Persians, keeps praying to his God three times a day although a royal decree has made it a crime. His enemies report him, and the king, who loves Daniel, cannot revoke his own law. Daniel is thrown to the lions and a stone is sealed over the mouth of the den. At dawn the king runs to the den and calls out: “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God whom you faithfully serve been able to deliver you from the lions?” And Daniel answers: “My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths so that they would not hurt me.” He comes up unharmed, “because he had trusted in his God.” The scene speaks of Easter: a stone sealed, a long night, a hurried dawn visit, and the servant of God alive. The reading ends grimly with the punishment of the accusers, as the law of that ancient kingdom demanded; Christ has taught us instead to pray for those who persecute us, and the martyrs, St George among them, died forgiving.

The Acts of the Apostles takes us to the first martyrdom among the twelve. “About that time King Herod laid violent hands upon some who belonged to the church. He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.” Seeing that this won him favour with some, he arrested Peter too, during the days of Unleavened Bread, intending to bring him out after the Passover. Herod, Agrippa I, was a ruler anxious to please, and Luke shows a politician's calculation; the Church does not read this as blame on the Jewish people, from whom the apostles themselves came. Then comes the verse that has carried the Church through every persecution: “While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.” James gave his life; Peter was released by an angel; both were held in the Church's prayer. In his letter to the Corinthians Paul reveals the secret of such courage. He had been caught up in visions, yet God left him “a thorn… in the flesh” and would not remove it. Three times he begged the Lord, and the answer came: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” So Paul concludes: “whenever I am weak, then I am strong.” Martyrs are not people without fear. They are weak people who have let the power of the Risen Christ dwell in them.

The Gospel states the cost plainly: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me… and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” These are hard words in a culture like ours, where family is everything. Jesus does not ask us to love our families less; he asks to be loved first, so that our love for them may be pure and strong. Then he gives the law of Easter: “Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.” George lost his rank, his safety and his life, and found them all again in the Risen Lord; seventeen centuries later we still keep his day. Most of us will not be asked to die for Christ. But we are asked every day to lose a little life for him: to refuse a dishonest deal, to keep Sunday holy when work demands it, to stand by the faith in an office or a college where it is mocked. The Gospel ends with a tender promise: even “a cup of cold water” given to one of Christ's little ones will not lose its reward. On this feast we pray for Cardinal Mar George Alencherry, Major Archbishop emeritus, for all bishops, priests and faithful who bear the name of St George, and for Christians who are persecuted today, that they may be strong in weakness, as he was.
conn: They shut the mouths of lions.
The heroes of faith “through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions” (Hebrews 11:33).
“The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them” (Psalm 34:7); an angel later frees Peter from prison (Acts 12:6–11).
Jesus had asked James and John, “Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?” and told them, “The cup that I drink you will drink” (Mark 10:38–39).
“He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless” (Isaiah 40:29).
“If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24), one of the longer forms given for today.
“Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10); “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom 3:1).
altar: The martyrs have always been honoured at the altar: their witness flows from the Sacrifice of Christ, whom they followed to the end. At the Holy Qurbana we offer the same Sacrifice and ask to share their courage.
The Body and Blood of the Risen Lord are the strength of the weak: in Communion his power comes to dwell in us, as Paul says, so that we too may stand firm.
outline: A soldier with everything to lose, and the name Geevarghese in Kerala homes.
Point 1 · The God who shut the lions' mouths
Daniel's faithful prayer and the sealed stone.
James killed, Peter imprisoned, the community on its knees.
Point 3 · Power made perfect in weakness
Paul's thorn and the secret of the martyrs.
Point 4 · Lose your life to find it
Christ loved first, and the cup of cold water.
A small boy named Geevarghese lighting a candle before the saint's image, and his grandmother teaching him whose name he bears.
live: Keep three short moments of prayer today, morning, noon and night, whatever else happens.
Pray a decade of the rosary for Christians in prison or danger for their faith.
Name one weakness you are ashamed of and give it to Christ: Lord, let your power dwell here.
Do one small, hidden kindness today for someone who cannot repay you.
fathers: It is not the punishment but the cause that makes the martyr. Many suffer; the martyr suffers for Christ and for the truth. Let us not admire only their blood, but the faith for which it was shed, and imitate that faith in our own trials.

Paul did not say, My grace takes away your weakness, but, My grace is sufficient for you. The thorn remained, so that the power might be seen to be God's. When we are weak and still stand, everyone sees that it is grace that holds us up.
magis: Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the Church has painstakingly collected the records of those who persevered to the end in witnessing to their faith.
When the Church keeps the memorials of martyrs and other saints during the annual cycle, she proclaims the Paschal mystery in those who have suffered and have been glorified with Christ.
Only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God's almighty power; this faith glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ's power.
The saints in heaven do not cease to intercede for us with the Father; their fraternal concern is the greatest help to our weakness.
Respect for parents and family is a duty; yet the first vocation of the Christian is to follow Jesus, and family ties, though important, are not absolute.

2027-04-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you gave St George the courage to choose you above his rank, his safety and his life. By his prayers, strengthen all who suffer for your name. As you shut the lions' mouths for Daniel and answered the prayer of the Church for Peter, protect your Church today. Let your power be made perfect in our weakness, so that we may love you first, take up our cross and find our life in you. Bless Cardinal Mar George Alencherry and all who bear the name of St George. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

Acts: Herod killed James and imprisoned Peter, and the Church prayed fervently for him.

2027-04-24.action: Pray today for Christians who are persecuted for their faith.
2027-04-24.question: What am I unwilling to lose for Christ?
kidsaint: George was a soldier, brave and strong. When the emperor ordered everyone to give up Jesus, George said no. He was put to death because he loved Jesus more than anything. Later people told a story of George fighting a dragon: it shows that faith in Jesus is stronger than every evil. Lesson: real bravery means staying close to Jesus even when it is hard!
2027-04-24.special: St George, Martyr (Geevarghese Sahada). Fourth Saturday of Resurrection.
term: The Syriac word for martyr, literally ‘witness’, like the Greek martyr. St George is called Mar Geevarghese Sahada. A martyr is one who bears witness to Christ by accepting death rather than deny him; the Church honours the martyrs' days as their true birthdays into heaven.

family.explain: Daniel kept praying to God even when the king's law said he must not. So he was thrown into a den full of hungry lions! All night the king could not sleep. In the morning he ran to the den, and Daniel was alive: God had sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths. St George was brave like Daniel: he would not stop loving Jesus, even when soldiers threatened him. Today we celebrate his feast.
family.intention: We pray for children and families in places where it is dangerous to be a Christian.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there a time when it is hard for you to say you love Jesus? Let us ask St George to make us brave.”

illus: A young woman from Kottayam, a nurse in a hospital abroad, was told by her supervisor that she must stop wearing the small cross she always wore under her collar. She was frightened: her family depended on her salary. That night she remembered the feast of St George at her home parish, and the old priest saying that martyrs were ordinary people who had decided whom they loved most. The next day she went to the supervisor, politely explained what the cross meant to her, and asked whether she could keep it hidden under her uniform. The supervisor agreed. She said later, “It was a small thing. But I learned that I could be weak and faithful at the same time.”

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you made St George strong in weakness. Gather us now in your presence, and give us his courage and his love for you. Amen. Alleluia!
share: O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God whom you faithfully serve been able to deliver you from the lions? (Daniel 6:20). When has God delivered me?
While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him (Acts 12:5). For whom should our community pray fervently now?
My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). What weakness of mine can I offer to Christ?
Those who lose their life for my sake will find it (Matthew 10:39). What is Jesus asking me to let go of?
pm.resp: Lord, make us strong in our weakness.
interc: For Christians who are persecuted, imprisoned or threatened for their faith, that the Risen Lord may strengthen and protect them.
For Cardinal Mar George Alencherry, Major Archbishop emeritus, and for all bishops, priests and faithful who bear the name of St George.
For soldiers, police and all who serve in uniform, that they may be just and brave.
For those who are afraid to speak of their faith at work or in college, that they may find courage.
For our families, that we may love Christ first and so love one another more truly.
pm.close: Father, you gave St George the grace to bear witness to your Son even to death. By his intercession, make us faithful witnesses in our own trials, strong in weakness and steadfast in love. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, today we keep the feast of Mar Geevarghese Sahada, St George the Martyr, whose name is carried by so many of our families and churches.

History tells us little, but enough: George was a soldier who refused to deny Christ in the persecution under Diocletian, and he was put to death, probably at the beginning of the fourth century. His tomb at Lydda was honoured by pilgrims. The dragon story came later; it is a legend that shows the victory of faith over evil.

Daniel too chose God above the king's law. Thrown to the lions, he was found alive at dawn, “because he had trusted in his God.” A sealed stone, a long night, a dawn visit, and the servant of God alive: it sounds like Easter.

In Acts, Herod kills James and imprisons Peter, and “the church prayed fervently to God for him.” The Church has always carried its martyrs and prisoners in prayer. Let us do the same today for Christians who suffer for their faith.

Paul reveals the secret of courage. He begged God to take away his thorn, and heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” Martyrs are not people without fear; they are weak people in whom the power of Christ lives.

Jesus says: “those who lose their life for my sake will find it.” Most of us will not be asked to die, but we are asked every day to lose a little life for him. Let us ask St George to make us brave, and pray for all who bear his name. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, St George was a brave soldier who loved Jesus more than anything. He would not give up Jesus, even when he was threatened.
You can be brave like St George: say your prayers, tell the truth, and be kind even when it is hard!
